one_liner: A wide-moat business worth owning, but it trades at 5.4x fair value. Interesting below about $40.

profile.what: Texas Instruments makes analog and embedded-processing chips: the tens of thousands of power-management, signal and control chips inside cars, factory equipment, appliances and electronics.
profile.money: It sells huge volumes of low-cost chips to more than 100,000 customers, mostly industrial and automotive, largely through its own website. It manufactures in its own factories on 300-millimetre wafers, which lowers unit cost, and is spending heavily to expand them.
profile.valued: TI is valued on free cash flow per share, the measure management itself targets, and on its dividend record. Today's heavy factory spending depresses free cash flow, so the stock depends on investors believing that cash will return once spending falls.

summary.sentence: A durable analog-chip franchise in the middle of an expensive factory build-out.
strengths: Long product lives and a very diverse customer base.
Free cash flow should rise as capex falls.
risks: Free cash flow fell sharply during the factory build-out.

meaning.what_it_does: Makes analog and embedded chips used in cars, factories and everyday electronics.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Sells tens of thousands of low-cost chips to more than 100,000 customers.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: Products sell for a decade or more, and it makes them in its own low-cost factories.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: A long industrial downturn, or Chinese analog chipmakers undercutting prices.

moat.summary: Analog chips are designed in for years and rarely redesigned out; in-house 300mm manufacturing lowers cost.

industry.summary: Unlike digital chips, analog designs change slowly and stay in production for decades.

management.summary: Runs the business explicitly for free cash flow per share; recent heavy factory investment has depressed it.

valuation.method: Fair value is the average of two methods: (1) Owner cash flow: $1.6B a year: free cash flow less stock-based pay (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM). (2) Damodaran: cash flow to the firm: Sales grow 5–11% for five years, fading to 3%; operating margin held at 36%; cost of capital 9.4%. Cash added, debt subtracted. The owner cash flow method grows the cash for five years, then at half that rate, 3% after year ten, discounted at 10%. Stock-based pay is deducted because it is a real cost to owners.
